notes:
I found sources for every verse. Here are the main gaps:

- **Gaps:** I didn't get to read Gill, Ellicott's full notes, the Pulpit Commentary, Wesley's Notes, Haydock (Catholic), Kretzmann (Lutheran), or anything on newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, lcms.org, 1517.org or the Pentecostal sites.
- **Traditions:** I found no real disagreements between Protestant traditions in this chapter. The only differences I found are in how far v. 15 points past its own time (see v. 15).
- **Popular teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so there is nothing on them below.

**v. 1**
- "Burden" (massa) comes from a verb meaning "to lift up" or "to carry." It means a weighty message revealed by God for the prophet to proclaim. A "vision" means Nahum in some way *saw* what he wrote. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- Nahum's name means "comfort." Nineveh had repented under Jonah about 100 years earlier but slipped back into sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- Matthew Henry calls the oracle a millstone hung round Nineveh's neck. It was written down so that later readers could check the event against the prediction. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Nah/Nah_001.cfm
- Constable notes that "Nineveh" sometimes stands for the whole Assyrian empire. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nahum-1.html
- Where Elkosh was is unknown. Galilee (Jerome, via JFB) and a village near Mosul are both suggested. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nahum/1-1.htm ; https://bible.org/article/introduction-book-nahum
- Barnes sees a further meaning: Nineveh as a type of the world at the final judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nahum/1-1.htm

**v. 2**
- God's jealousy is "love in action." He is jealous *for* us, not *of* us (Redpath, quoted by Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- The Gospel Coalition: God demands total allegiance and exclusive worship. The verb forms for "vengeance" describe God's consistent, habitual way of acting. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nahum/
- Henry: God's "fury" is not uncontrolled passion as it is in humans. It suits a righteous God and gives his justice an edge. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Nah/Nah_001.cfm
- Calvin: Nahum takes his picture of God from Exodus 34. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm

**v. 3**
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): God has never pardoned a sin without it being punished. Every sin is paid for, either in hell or at the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- The Gospel Coalition: God is patient because he is powerful, not weak. "If he had less power, he would be less patient." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nahum/
- Calvin: "slow to anger" answers the ungodly who mocked God's warnings by appealing to his mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm
- Constable: God's patience explains why Assyria was allowed to abuse Israel for so long. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nahum-1.html

**v. 4**
- This may allude to God drying up the Red Sea and the Jordan. Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon are named because they were famous for fertility. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nahum/
- Clarke: vv. 3–6 show God controlling all of nature. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/nahum-1.html
- NET note: some scholars want to change the first "withers" to another verb so the acrostic gets its missing letter. NET advises leaving the Hebrew as it is. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Nah+1%3A2-4

**v. 5**
- Calvin: mountains stand only as long as God holds them up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm
- Coffman: the verse points to earthquakes and volcanoes, and to a sin-cursed earth that is hostile to rebels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/nahum-1.html

**v. 6**
- Constable: the Hebrew word for indignation means boiling rage. Nahum is not teaching that God's enemies are annihilated, only that no one survives his unchecked wrath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nahum-1.html
- Guzik: God's patience should make people quick to repent, not careless about it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/

**v. 7**
- Spurgeon (via Guzik): it is only a "day" of trouble, so it will end. "Knows" means loving communion with those who trust him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- The Gospel Coalition: the Lord who sends the wrath is also the only refuge from it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nahum/
- Calvin: calling God good answers any charge that he is too severe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm
- Coffman: God is good by nature, a refuge, and he knows his people with covenant love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/nahum-1.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik, quoting Boice: the flood came true literally. Heavy rains broke down Nineveh's walls, and the city was lost until the 1840s. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- Preceptaustin quotes Badger: a layer of pebbles and sand found in the mounds fits the flood. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nahum-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations
- Clarke: "darkness" means calamity. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/nahum-1.html
- Calvin: "her place" means the very ground of the city will be destroyed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm
- Constable, citing Johnston: Nahum's curses may echo the brutal Assyrian treaty curses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nahum-1.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik: trouble won't come "a second time" because the first blow will be complete. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- Calvin agrees: one blow and the ruin is total. He notes that some others read the verse as God limiting Judah's suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm
- Coffman, following Hailey: it is probably addressed to both Assyria and Judah, and in the end to all humanity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/nahum-1.html

**v. 10**
- Dry stubble burns at the smallest flame, which shows how ready Nineveh was for judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- A devotional on preceptaustin: the enemies are caught in their own traps and made drunk by their own wine. They reap what they sow. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61869/

**v. 11**
- Who the plotter is remains uncertain. Some say Sennacherib. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61869/
- Calvin: the plot was against God himself, not just against Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm
- Henry: the Assyrians' letters put God on a level with pagan gods. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Nah/Nah_001.cfm

**v. 12**
- Constable: this is the only "Thus says the LORD" in the book. "No longer" means Judah would not be afflicted *by Assyria*, since other nations did afflict it later. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nahum-1.html
- Calvin: the verse speaks to both Israel and Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/nahum/1.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik applies it today: believers can ask God to break the yoke of sin, if they are willing to walk in the freedom he gives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- Constable lists the yoke as one of the book's Assyrian conquest images. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nahum-1.html

**v. 14**
- The Gospel Coalition: this is a threefold sentence on the king. He will have no heirs, his idols will be shown powerless, and he will have a shameful grave. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nahum/
- JFB and Poole connect it to the murder of Sennacherib. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nahum/1-1.htm
- Clarke reads "no more of thy name be sown" as no more of Judah being carried into captivity. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/nahum-1.html
- Layman's Bible Commentary: God strikes at power, life, family name and religion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/nahum-1.html

**v. 15** (this is where readings differ most)
- **Historical reading:** the messengers bring news that Nineveh has fallen (Clarke). Henry pictures runners arriving after a long run of bad news. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nahum/1-15.html
- **Gospel reading:** Barnes applies the verse in part to every gospel preacher. Guzik links it to Isaiah 52:7. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nahum/1-15.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nahum-1/
- The Pulpit Commentary, writing on Isaiah 52:7, sees a second, Messianic meaning (Romans 10:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/52-7.html
- **Future-kingdom reading:** Kelly and Chuck Smith place it in the coming kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nahum/1-15.html
- **Feasts:** Coffman criticises scholars who claim Nahum cared nothing for moral values because he mentions the feasts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/nahum-1.html
- **Catholic translations:** the Douay-Rheims has "Belial" where others have "the wicked." https://biblehub.com/catholic/nahum/1-15.htm
- **Modern theory:** Layman's mentions the idea that Nahum was written for a New Year festival after Nineveh fell in 612. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/nahum-1.html

**Modern scholarship on vv. 2–8 (the acrostic)**
- Verses 2–8 are a partial, broken alphabet poem running only from the first Hebrew letter to the eleventh. NET calls the Divine Warrior picture its theme. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Nah+1%3A2-4
- Older critics dated the poem late and saw it as added by a later editor. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=nahum ; https://bible.org/seriespage/1-nahum
- Evangelical writers reply that rebuilding a full acrostic is guesswork with no manuscript support. https://bible.org/article/book-nahum
- Constable: the victory hymn is sung *before* the battle. The half-alphabet may suggest "more judgment still to come." https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/nahum-1.html
- Longman (cited at TGC) thinks the broken pattern supports the message. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/nahum/
